nameStory: Heath wood-rush gets its name from its love of open, heathland areas and woodland edges where it forms small tufts among other low-growing plants. The 'wood-rush' part comes from its grass-like appearance and preference for woodlands, even though it's not actually a true rush or grass but belongs to the rush family.
description: Heath wood-rush is a small, unassuming plant that looks like a delicate grass at first glance but belongs to the rush family. It grows 4-16 inches tall in neat little clumps with narrow leaves sprouting from the base. In late spring and early summer, it sends up slender stems topped with clusters of tiny, dark brown to black flowers that later turn into round seed capsules.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves with distinctive long white hairs along the edges that you can easily see and feel - run your finger along a leaf margin and you'll feel these soft, silky fringes

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers clustered at stem tips, each with six dark brown to black tepals (petal-like parts) that feel papery and scale-like to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, neat tufts or clumps with leaves emerging from the base, creating a fountain-like appearance that's more delicate than most grasses

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, brown capsules replace the flowers in late spring, containing small, shiny seeds that rattle softly when the capsule is shaken

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves often turn reddish or bronze-colored when stressed by drought or cold, giving the plant a distinctive rusty appearance

habitat: Heath wood-rush prefers upland woodland areas, forest edges, and clearings with well-drained, often acidic soils. Unlike most plants in the rush family that love wet areas, this species thrives in drier woodland settings and open heathlands. You'll often find it growing alongside blueberries, bracken fern, and other acid-loving plants in partially shaded to sunny spots.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh green leaves showing their characteristic white-fringed edges. Flower clusters begin developing in late spring with tiny dark blooms.
seasonality.summer: Flowers mature into round seed capsules by early summer. The plant maintains its neat, clumped appearance throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves often take on reddish or bronze tones as temperatures drop. The plant begins to slow its growth as it prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Leaves may persist through mild winters, often with a reddish tinge, though the plant appears dormant with dried seed heads still visible on stems.

funFact: Despite looking exactly like a grass, heath wood-rush is actually more closely related to lilies than to any grass - it has the same six-part flower structure as a lily, just shrunk down to tiny proportions and colored brown instead of showy petals!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with field wood-rush and other small grasses, but the telltale white hairs along the leaf edges are your best clue - run your finger along any suspected wood-rush leaf and you'll feel those distinctive soft fringes that grasses lack.
contextualKnowledge: The taxonomy of wood-rushes has been notoriously unstable, with heath wood-rush previously lumped together with several other species or classified as varieties of European species. Some debate still exists about whether it's truly native to North America or introduced, though most botanists now consider it a native circumpolar species.
compareHints: Heath wood-rush differs from field woodrush by having flower clusters on variable-length stalks rather than in tight, rounded heads. Compared to hairy woodrush, it's generally smaller and has less prominent leaf hairs. The key to separating wood-rush species is examining the flower cluster arrangement and the density of leaf hairs under close inspection.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Hairy woodrush is distinguished from other New England woodrushes primarily by its prominent white hairs along the leaf edges - field woodrush has much less noticeable hairs, while heath woodrush tends to grow in more open, acidic areas.
Unlike other New England woodrushes that grow in lower elevation forests and fields, spiked woodrush is the high-altitude specialist of the group.
Small-flower woodrush lives up to its name with much smaller, less noticeable flowers than other New England woodrushes.
**[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Bulbous woodrush stands apart from other New England woodrushes primarily by its distinctive bulbous base structures, which other species lack.
White woodrush differs from other New England woodrushes by its whitish flowers (rather than brown or reddish) and preference for oak forests specifically.
Field woodrush is the most common and widespread woodrush in New England, distinguished from its relatives by its preference for open, sunny habitats rather than shady woods.
